header:
Date: 2027-02-16 | Time: 14:00-14:47 UTC | Duration: 47m
Redwood: Samira Khan (AE), Jordan Lee (SE)
CatalystCommerce: Maya Patel (PM), Ravi Desai (Lead Eng), Lena Ortiz (Data Scientist)
transcript:
[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check — we have 47 minutes on the calendar, we'll go through last week's results, then Jordan will walk through the SDK snippets for function and tool calls and the structured-output schema.
[00:18] Maya: Sounds good, and hi Samira, hi Jordan. We ran the light bench from last time, shared the spreadsheet in the drive. There were some weird outputs on the invoice extraction where address fields came back in a nested list.
[00:35] Jordan: Yep I saw that — looks like the structured-output parser we shipped in the initial snippet didn't enforce the top-level keys strictly. The model was sometimes returning arrays for fields we expected as strings.
[00:50] Ravi: Right, when we validated against our golden set, about 8% of responses failed schema checks, mostly on address and line_item arrays. Also saw longer token counts than expected on long receipts which pushed latency up.
[01:10] Samira: Thanks for the color. Two things we want to call out: one is the SDK function-calling example we updated last night to include explicit JSON schema validation on the client side; two is using Redwood's structured_output param which can be stricter if you pass a schema. We'll walk through both.
[01:34] Jordan: I'll share screen in a sec — but quick note, the SDK has two helpers: callFunction() which attaches a function contract and validateOutput() which runs a JSON schema check locally. Some customers disable client-side validation to save CPU, but we generally recommend validating before ingestion.
[01:52] Lena: Is validateOutput part of the hosted SDK or the node helper? We're using Python on the backend.
[02:00] Jordan: It's in all official SDKs; for Python it's validate_output(payload, schema). There was one naming mismatch — the SDK example used 'structuredOutput' key but the model sometimes returned 'structured_output' — casing issues from the LLM. We added a normalization step.
[02:20] Maya: That's probably what tripped us up. We saw a few outputs where the model returned camelCase instead of snake_case.
[02:27] Samira: We've seen transcription of model behavior like that too — small variations. The current recommendation is: include a strict JSON schema with required fields and types, then run the SDK validator which will attempt normalization and surface precise errors.
[02:45] Ravi: On latency — our staging test shows median token latency is fine (90ms per token), but 95th is 780ms which occasionally breaches our target of 500ms for the interactive flow. Are we seeing batching effects or KV cache warm starts?
[03:05] Jordan: Two likely contributors: KV cache warm-up when long context hits, and batching on the Redwood hosted endpoint which is throughput-optimized. For interactive app flows you can pin to a lower batch size or use dedicated pool which reduces tail latency. There's also prefix caching; if you can isolate repeated prompts, the tail drops.
[03:26] Maya: For the POC our success criteria says 95th < 500ms for the checkout pathway, so we might need to look at dedicated or a routing policy. What are the implications for cost?
[03:39] Samira: Dedicated reduces 95th but costs more — typically a reserved GPU pool. We can give an estimate based on your request volume; Jordan can run a quick cost model with your sample traffic.
[03:51] Jordan: Yep I can plug the 10 TPS sample from your sheet into the batching model. Quick aside, there was a prompt engineering tweak — using shorter system instructions and moving user context into external metadata reduced token growth by ~12% in our tests.
[04:10] Ravi: Good to know. On the schema failures — when address came back as an array we saw our downstream parser crash because it assumed a single string. Could we get the SDK to coerce arrays to strings if single-element?
[04:24] Jordan: The validator has an option coerce_single_array true which flattens single-item arrays into scalar. It's off by default because coercion can mask real errors. But for pragmatic POC you can enable it. We'll include that in the snippet.
[04:38] Lena: Also, some of our tests expect amounts in cents integer — the model sometimes returns a formatted string like '$12.34'. We had to post-process. Can we enforce numeric types?
[04:50] Samira: Yes, the schema can require integer type and the validator will fail otherwise. In addition we recommend canonicalization hooks in the SDK — small functions to normalize currency fields. Jordan will include examples.
[05:06] Jordan: I'll paste a short Python snippet now — not perfect transcript but gist: 

def call_and_validate(client, prompt, schema):
    resp = client.call_function(
        model='redwood-optimized-neo',
        function='extract_invoice',
        prompt=prompt,
        structured_output=true,
        schema=schema,
        max_tokens=512
    )
    # resp.output could be camelCase or snake_case
    normalized = client.normalize_keys(resp.output)
    validation = client.validate_output(normalized, schema, coerce_single_array=true)
    return normalized, validation

[06:00] Maya: That looks straightforward. We'll try it in our integration test harness. A question about tool-calling — we want the model to call an internal microservice to fetch product metadata. Does Redwood's tool call map to our internal API directly or do we need an adapter?
[06:18] Jordan: It's an adapter. The SDK emits a structured function call payload which you can map to your internal API. Example: function: get_product(id) args: {"id":"1234"}. Your service should validate and return JSON, which the SDK then passes back to the model as tool output.
[06:35] Ravi: Any concerns about auth headers or KMS with tool calls? We run internal services behind mTLS.
[06:42] Samira: Tool calls do not cross Redwood — the SDK handles them in your environment. So auth stays internal. If you route through Redwood for managed connectors that's a different path and involves credentials in the customer-managed vault. For POC you can keep calls in your network.
[06:58] Lena: Great. On the structured output schema we discussed having an examples array of golden outputs so the validator can run fuzzy checks; does the SDK support example-based checks?
[07:10] Jordan: Not baked into the validator, but you can easily add an examples step: compare similarity against golden outputs using embeddings. We can add a quick script that runs an embedding similarity threshold.
[07:22] Maya: That would be helpful — our PM wants both strict schema and similarity score.
[07:28] Samira: We'll attach an examples-based check to the validation flow. Jordan will send the script.
[07:36] Ravi: A couple of minor transcribe notes — sometimes model output includes extra commentary like 'note: inferred' which breaks downstream. Can we strip meta fields?
[07:48] Jordan: You can include 'no_extraneous_text' in the system instruction, and the structured_output flag reduces free text. But not perfect; validator can also fail on extra keys if you set 'additionalProperties': false in the schema.
[08:03] Maya: Security question from our legal: we need SOC 2 plus audit logs for any production. For the pilot we need to know retention and SSO options.
[08:12] Samira: We are SOC 2 Type II, and for hosted we provide audit logs and configurable retention. For private deployments (VPC/on-prem) you get full control and can integrate with your KMS/HSM. We'll share the security pack.
[08:30] Lena: And SSO? We use Okta.
[08:34] Samira: Yes SAML/Okta supported. We'll include instructions.
[08:40] Ravi: Back to results — can we go over the failure examples in the spreadsheet? I pulled three representative hits.
[08:47] Jordan: Sure — first example, invoice with line_items as a top-level array of objects but the model returned a single object with line_items collapsed into a string. Looks like the prompt asked for 'a concise list' so it summarized. In the prompt we should instruct 'return machine-readable JSON only' and attach schema.
[09:09] Maya: We did attach schema but maybe the schema wasn't required in the model call?
[09:14] Jordan: In your first run the schema was passed as a comment in the prompt rather than the structured_output param; the model respected it less. The SDK param 'schema' enforces stronger behavior.
[09:26] Ravi: Understood. We'll re-run with the SDK's structured_output hook.
[09:30] Samira: Great. Also a note on tokenization: you can reduce tokens by compressing system messages and moving large product catalogs to an external DB reference. The model doesn't need the whole catalog inline.
[09:44] Maya: We're testing one-shot generation for the checkout summary; anything to help ensure determinism?
[09:49] Jordan: Lower temperature and use function calling where possible; function outputs are deterministic if the model doesn't add noise. Also consider n_best=1 and ensure max_tokens is tight.
[09:58] Lena: Any gotchas we should watch for during the 1k sample run?
[10:02] Jordan: Look at distribution of failures, token counts, and whether errors correlate with certain invoice templates. Also check for casing differences and currency formats.
[10:12] Ravi: We'll do that. If we still can't get 95th < 500ms, what's the trade path? Dedicated? Private?
[10:18] Samira: If cost permits, move to Redwood Dedicated which gives reserved capacity and lower tail latency. If you need on-prem for compliance, Redwood Private is available but has longer setup time. We can run a short cost / latency model and present options.
[10:33] Maya: Okay. A couple admin items: Samira, can you send the SDK snippet, validator script, and the security pack?
[10:41] Samira: Yes — I'll bundle SDK snippets (Python + Node), the validator and the security pack. Jordan will add the examples similarity script.
[10:49] Jordan: Also sharing a quick benchmark harness — it's a small load tester that hits the endpoint and produces latency percentiles. Use it with a test API key.
[10:58] Ravi: We'll run in staging. Any preferences on how we share results? Slack channel or drive?
[11:03] Maya: Drive is fine, and Slack for quick notes.
[11:07] Samira: Perfect. Before we wrap, any blockers?
[11:10] Ravi: No blockers beyond the load test and schema tweaks. We'll correlate failures with templates and report.
[11:16] Lena: One more question — function calls sometimes return tool output that the model misinterprets; should we canonicalize tool responses?
[11:23] Jordan: Yes canonicalization is ideal: ensure your tool returns strict JSON with types matching the function contract. Avoid free text.
[11:30] Maya: Great. Let's recap next steps.
[11:33] Samira: Quick recap: Jordan sends validator + examples similarity script; Samira sends SDK snippets + pricing + security pack; Catalyst to run 1k benchmark and share results; follow-up architecture review if we can't meet 95th latency target. We'll schedule a cadence for next week.
[11:53] Maya: Thanks everyone.
[11:55] Samira: Thanks, talk soon.
[12:00] (call ends)
